# Introduction

The analysis of psychotic discourse has long occupied a complex position at the intersection of clinical description, theoretical interpretation, and linguistic observation. Classical approaches, particularly within psychoanalysis and phenomenology, have emphasized the meaningful and structured character of delusional experience, often treating it as a coherent, if unconventional, form of world-construction [@freud1911a; @sass1994b]. At the same time, traditions emerging from communication theory, most notably the work of Bateson and the Palo Alto group, have foregrounded the relational and pragmatic dimensions of disturbed communication, highlighting how paradox, meta-communication, and breakdowns in contextual framing may contribute to the emergence and stabilization of psychotic patterns [@bateson1969b; @bateson1972a; @bateson1987e; @bateson1987d; @watzlawickp.1967].

Despite their differences, these perspectives share a common assumption: that psychotic discourse exhibits an underlying form of organization, whether conceived as symbolic coherence, altered subjectivity, or disturbed communicative structure. Yet the nature of this organization, and in particular its temporal properties, has rarely been examined in a systematic and empirically grounded manner. Much of the existing literature relies on close reading, case-based interpretation, or theoretical reconstruction, leaving open the question of how discursive features unfold across extended narrative material and whether their relationships remain stable over time.

The present study addresses this gap by proposing a reproducible computational framework for the analysis of psychotic discourse, grounded in the interaction between two theoretically informed dimensions: meta-communication and delusional ontology. The notion of meta-communication, derived from Bateson’s work, refers to signals that frame, qualify, or comment upon the communicative act itself, thereby establishing the conditions under which meaning is to be interpreted. In the context of psychosis, disruptions or amplifications of such framing processes have been hypothesized to play a central role in the emergence of paradoxical or self-referential communication. Delusional ontology, by contrast, captures the explicit construction of an alternative reality, encompassing beliefs about external agents, metaphysical structures, and the nature of existence itself, as extensively documented in both psychoanalytic and phenomenological accounts [@freud1911a; @sass1994b].

While these dimensions have traditionally been treated qualitatively, the present approach operationalizes them as paragraph-level textual features, enabling their systematic measurement and temporal analysis. By combining these features into a coupling index, the study examines not only their co-occurrence but also their dynamic relationship across the progression of a narrative. This allows for the empirical evaluation of competing models of psychotic discourse, including the hypothesis of cumulative escalation, the possibility of temporally clustered intensification, and the alternative view that discursive organization may be locally contingent and episodic.

All analyses were conducted in R [@rcoreteam2025], using *quanteda* for text processing [@benoit2018b] and *quanteda.textstats* for lexical-statistical measures [@benoit2024a], with data manipulation implemented through *dplyr* [@wickham2026c] and visualization performed using *ggplot2* [@wickham2016].

The empirical material for this investigation is Daniel Paul Schreber’s *Memoirs of My Nervous Illness* [@schreber1903a], a canonical text in the study of psychosis that has been extensively interpreted across multiple theoretical traditions. Unlike many previous analyses, the present study is based on a digitally reconstructed and manually curated version of the text, derived from OCR processing and subsequently reduced to the core narrative content. This procedure aimed to minimize editorial noise and peripheral material, thereby enhancing the validity of paragraph-level segmentation and feature extraction.

Situating this work within the broader field of computational psychiatry, the study contributes to ongoing efforts to bridge qualitative theory and quantitative analysis by transforming complex clinical constructs into empirically testable variables [@huys2016a]. At the same time, it remains closely aligned with the conceptual insights of earlier traditions, particularly those of Bateson and the Palo Alto school, whose emphasis on meta-communication and contextual framing finds here a formal and operational extension. In doing so, the study seeks not to replace interpretative approaches but to complement them with a methodological framework capable of revealing patterns that may otherwise remain implicit.

By examining the temporal organization of meta-communication and delusional ontology in Schreber’s text, this study advances a central question: whether psychotic discourse is best understood as a continuously structured system or as a dynamically shifting field characterized by localized moments of intensified organization. The answer to this question has implications not only for theoretical models of psychosis but also for the broader understanding of how meaning is constructed, disrupted, and reconfigured in extreme forms of human experience.
